chapters.title: A Package for a Dead Man
chapters.text:
The bell over the bookshop door jingled just after ten, and a courier in a damp brown jacket shuffled in with a parcel tucked under his arm. Winnie Calloway looked up from her cocoa and her crossword. Hattie Bramble, who had popped next door with a plate of cinnamon twists, set the plate down at once.

"Delivery for Mr. Lionel Crane," the courier said, reading from his clipboard. "The inn sent me here. They said the bookshop takes in packages for guests." Winnie and Hattie exchanged a look. Nobody had told the poor young man. Winnie signed for it with a sigh, and the courier hurried back out into the drizzle, none the wiser.

The parcel came from a publisher in New York. Hattie knew perfectly well that it ought to go straight to Sam. Still, the flap had come unstuck in the rain, and a thick sheaf of papers had slid halfway out on its own. It seemed only polite to tuck them back in, and impossible not to read the first page while doing so.

It was a contract for a brand new cookbook, to be written by Lionel Crane and Lionel Crane alone. There was no mention of an assistant, a helper, or anyone else at all. Biscuit, who had followed Hattie over, sat on the counter and sniffed the corner of the package.

"Whose recipes, I wonder," Hattie murmured, and she copied the title into her little green notebook.

chapters.title: The Harbor Master Confesses
chapters.text:
Hattie found Gordon Pike in the harbor office, staring at a mug of coffee that had long since gone cold. Outside, the gulls wheeled over the fishing boats, and a foghorn moaned from somewhere past the lighthouse. She set a warm blueberry muffin on his desk and waited. Thirty years of teaching had taught her that silence was often the best question.

Gordon lasted nearly a full minute. "It was the year my sister Margaret was so ill," he said at last, rubbing his weathered face. "She had entered her apple pie in the bake-off every autumn for twenty years and never won so much as a ribbon. I was on the committee. I moved a few numbers on the scorecards. She went home with the blue ribbon, and she was so happy, Hattie. She passed that winter." Hattie's heart softened, though her pencil kept moving in her green notebook.

"Lionel found out," Gordon went on. "Heaven knows how. He had a nose for scandal. He kept hinting he would mention it on his television show unless I made certain the committee did whatever he wanted. Better rooms, better seats, and his own way in everything."

"And now he cannot mention anything at all," Hattie said gently.

Gordon flushed red to his ears. "I know how that sounds. I did not hurt the man. But I will not pretend I am sorry he is quiet." He looked away, toward the rowboats bobbing by the pier.

chapters.title: Words Never Sent
chapters.text:
Dottie Quill had been asked to air out the Blue Suite, and she did not care to do it alone. "It gives me the shivers, Hattie," she confessed, handing over a feather duster. "All his things are still here, just as he left them."

Detective Hask had already carried off his suitcase and his travel kettle. What remained was a stack of glossy magazines, a silk dressing gown, and the old walnut writing desk by the window. Hattie dusted it slowly. One of the small drawers stuck, and when she gave it a patient wiggle, it slid open to reveal a single sheet of cream stationery.

It was a letter in Lionel's sharp, slanting hand, crossed out in places. It was addressed to Colette. "After twelve years," it read, "I have decided your services are no longer required. You will vacate your position at the end of the month. I trust you will not make a fuss." It was unsigned and undated, and it had plainly never been sent.

Hattie read it twice, and her throat tightened. What a cold way to end twelve years of anyone's life. Still, she reminded herself, it was one motive among several. Rupert had his debts, Gordon had his secret, Imogen had her inheritance, and poor Delia had her old grudge. She copied the letter word for word into her green notebook and slid the sheet back into its drawer.

"Find anything?" Dottie called from the hallway. "Something Sam ought to see," Hattie answered quietly.

chapters.title: Stay Out of It, Aunt Hattie
chapters.text:
Deputy Sam Bramble came through the back door of the Rolling Pin just as Hattie pulled a tray of apple turnovers from the oven. He took off his hat, which was never a good sign. Sam only took off his hat when he had something serious to say. "Aunt Hattie," he began, "I need you to stop poking around."

Hattie slid a turnover onto a plate and set it in front of him. "Poking? I deliver pastries, dear. I chat. It is called being neighborly."

"Detective Hask doesn't call it that." Sam sighed and broke the turnover in half, letting the steam curl up. "She's heard you've been in the potting shed, the laundry room, and now the Blue Suite. She asked me whether my aunt was running a private detective agency out of a bakery kitchen." Biscuit hopped onto the stool beside him and eyed the turnover hopefully.

"The county detective has made up her mind about Delia," Hattie said quietly. "That is exactly why someone needs to keep an open one."

Sam rubbed the back of his neck. "I know you mean well. But if you muddy things up, it could hurt Delia more than help her. Lorna Hask is sharp, and she plays by the book. Please, just bake your pies for a few days." Hattie patted his hand and refilled his coffee. She did not promise anything, and Sam, who had known her his whole life, noticed that she did not.

chapters.title: The Innkeeper's Fib
chapters.text:
Rupert Ashby was polishing brass in the front hall of the Gull's Rest Inn, rubbing the same doorknob over and over as if it had personally offended him. He gave Hattie a tired smile when she came in with the morning bread. "Terrible week," he said. "Guests are canceling left and right. Nobody wants to sleep where a famous man was poisoned." When Hattie gently pointed out that Lionel had fallen ill at the tea tent, not here, he only shook his head. "Try telling that to the newspapers." He set down his rag. "I've told the detective a dozen times. I was right here all morning, in my office, doing the accounts. I never left the building until the judging started."

Hattie tilted her head. She remembered that morning perfectly. She had arrived at dawn with a basket of croissants and rung the little silver bell on the front desk three times. Nobody had answered. And when she had walked back down the gravel drive, Rupert's green station wagon had been missing from its usual spot beside the hedge. "How odd," she said mildly. "I must have just missed you, then."

A flush crept up Rupert's neck. He began to scrub at the doorknob with new energy. "I might have stepped out for a moment. Errands. I don't recall exactly."

Hattie nodded as though that were the most natural thing in the world. Back on the sidewalk, she opened her green notebook and underlined his name twice.

chapters.title: A Scent in the Shed
chapters.text:
The potting shed smelled of damp earth and old clay pots, just as it had the first time. Hattie stepped inside with Biscuit at her heels and pulled the door nearly closed behind her. Rain drummed softly on the tin roof.

She was not entirely sure what she was looking for. Something about the empty hook had been nagging at her for days, the way a missing ingredient nags at a recipe. She stood very still beside the workbench and let her eyes wander over the coiled hoses, the seed trays, the cracked watering can, and the hook itself, still bare.

Then she noticed it. Beneath the earthy smell was something softer and sweeter, the faint perfume of lavender. It was not the garden kind, which grew by the stone wall outside and had long since gone to seed. This was the creamy, powdery scent of a good hand cream, the sort that came in a little tin and cost more than it ought to.

Hattie bent close to the workbench. The smell was strongest near a shelf of garden twine and on the doorframe, where someone might have steadied themselves. Someone with soft hands, she thought, who had cared enough to protect them before coming out to work among the thorns.

Biscuit sneezed twice, offended. "I agree," Hattie whispered. "Gardeners don't usually smell like a fancy shop." She wrote the word lavender in her notebook and drew a small circle around it.

chapters.title: A Fisherman's Word
chapters.text:
Abe Tolliver had been mending nets on the same weathered bench by the harbor for as long as Hattie could remember. He was eighty-one, deaf in one ear, and sharp as a fishhook in every other way. Hattie sat down beside him with a thermos of hot cider and two molasses cookies wrapped in wax paper. "You want to know about the painter girl," Abe said before she could even ask. "Whole village does."

Hattie admitted that she did. Imogen claimed she had been painting at the lighthouse that morning, and Abe always went out early. Abe chewed a cookie slowly, thinking. "Saw her, all right. Quarter past five, I'd say. I was rowing out to check my lobster traps, and there she was on the rocks with her easel, bundled up in that yellow slicker of hers. Hard to miss."

Hattie's heart lifted, but Abe wagged a crooked finger before she could say a word. "Don't go thinking she was there the whole morning. I was out past the point an hour, maybe more. When I came back in, the easel was still standing there, but I didn't see hide nor hair of her. Could have been inside the lighthouse. Could have been anywhere."

Hattie wrote it down carefully: seen at five, then not seen for at least an hour. An easel, after all, could stand by itself.

"Thank you, Abe," she said, pouring him more cider. He grunted and went back to his nets, humming an old sea shanty.

chapters.title: Biscuit Digs In
chapters.text:
Biscuit had never cared for leashes, but he tolerated his red harness on the walk past the Gull's Rest Inn, mostly because the walled garden was full of interesting smells. This morning he was more interested than usual. The moment Hattie let him through the gate, he tugged her straight toward a large blue hydrangea by the far wall.

"What is it, sweetheart?" Hattie asked. "A mouse?" Biscuit did not answer, being a cat. Instead he began to dig with great determination, flinging damp soil and brown petals onto Hattie's good walking shoes. She tried to tug him away, then stopped. The earth beneath the bush was loose and dark, as if someone had turned it over very recently.

Something metal glinted among the roots. Hattie knelt, wincing as her knees complained, and drew it out with two fingers wrapped in her handkerchief. It was a small garden trowel with a wooden handle, caked in mud. Someone had pushed it deep under the hydrangea, where nobody would ever think to look.

Hattie turned it over slowly. Bits of green leaf clung to the blade. She could not be sure, but they looked a great deal like the foxglove she had seen cut down by the wall.

She wrapped the trowel carefully and tucked it into her basket. Sam would scold her, but he would scold her far more if she left it there for the rain. "Good boy," she told Biscuit, who accepted the praise and a sardine treat as his due.

chapters.title: The Village Rallies
chapters.text:
The news spread across Pennywhistle Harbor before the church bell finished striking noon. Detective Lorna Hask had named Delia Fairweather a person of interest. By one o'clock, the Sugar and Spoon was as empty as a cookie jar after a church picnic.

Hattie watched from the window of the Rolling Pin, her hands on her hips. Across the square, Delia stood alone behind her glass counter, arranging and rearranging a tray of maple scones that nobody had come to buy. "That will not do," Hattie announced to no one in particular. Biscuit flicked an ear.

She marched next door to the bookshop, where Winnie Calloway was already reaching for her coat. "I know that look," Winnie said. "Who are we calling first?"

They called everyone. Winnie rang the knitting circle, the garden club, and her cousin who ran the post office. Hattie rang Oswald Finch at the library, who promised to bring the entire Thursday reading group. She even put a hand-lettered sign in her own window: Rolling Pin closed for one hour. Go buy a scone from Delia.

By three o'clock there was a line out the door of the Sugar and Spoon. Abe Tolliver bought six cinnamon buns. Dottie Quill bought a whole pie. Oswald Finch bought a lemon tart. Delia caught Hattie's eye through the crowd, her own eyes shining. Hattie simply winked. Some things a village could fix with a pie or two, even when it could not fix everything.

chapters.title: Small Muddy Boots
chapters.text:
It was nearly dusk when Hattie carried a box of day-old bread around to the back of the Gull's Rest Inn. Dottie liked to feed the crumbs to the sparrows, and Hattie hated waste. The back porch was a cluttered, friendly place, with a rocking chair, a stack of firewood, and a row of pegs for coats and umbrellas. Hattie set the box down by the screen door and was about to knock when something made her pause.

On a folded newspaper beneath the bench sat a pair of rubber garden boots, set out to dry. They were caked to the ankle in thick dark mud, the very same reddish mud that clung to the beds of the walled garden. What struck Hattie most was their size. They were small, much smaller than her own, the sort of boots that might fit a slender woman or a girl of twelve.

Rupert's feet were enormous. Gordon Pike wore size thirteen and complained about it constantly. Lionel, she recalled, had worn polished loafers and never set foot in soil if he could help it. Hattie leaned closer without touching them. A crushed purple petal was stuck to one heel.

"Those aren't mine," Dottie said, pushing open the screen door with a tea towel over her shoulder. "Been sitting there since the bake-off. I assumed one of the guests left them." Hattie smiled and handed her the bread. Then she wrote two words, small boots, in her notebook and underlined them.
